entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Cornell University, founded in 1865 in Ithaca, New York, by Ezra Cornell and Andrew Dickson White, was one of the first American universities to embrace the democratic principle that it would 'be an institution where any person can find instruction in any study' — a radical departure from elite liberal arts education that made it the template for America's land-grant universities. Cornell was among the first major American universities to admit women and students of any race from its founding.

Ezra Cornell, a telegraph magnate who co-founded Western Union, donated $500,000 and 200 acres for the university. Andrew Dickson White, the first president, designed Cornell as a secular, non-sectarian institution combining classical education with practical training in agriculture, engineering, and the sciences. The Land Grant Act of 1862 (Morrill Act) provided federal land to finance agricultural and technical colleges; Cornell used this to build a genuinely comprehensive university that mixed Latin with animal husbandry.

Cornell's 'any person, any study' principle produced extraordinary breadth: it remains one of the few Ivy League universities with colleges in agriculture, human ecology, industrial and labor relations, and veterinary medicine alongside liberal arts and engineering. Cornell's medical school in New York City, hotel administration school, law school, and tech campus in New York City (with Technion Israel) demonstrate this comprehensive vision. Notable alumni include Nobel Prize winners, two US vice presidents, and Warren Buffett's son Peter Cornell.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Cornell's founding principle of 'any person, any study' — admitting women, all races, and combining practical with classical education from 1865 — made it the democratic alternative to elite liberal arts education that shaped America's land-grant university system.
